piece.caption: How to protect your business WhatsApp Web account from hijacking and Boss Scam fraud. The Ministry of Home Affairs warned that simply closing a browser tab does not log you out of WhatsApp Web on office computers. Attackers are sending malicious ZIP files named Statement of Account to run malware, hijack active sessions, and demand urgent payment transfers from employees. Always log out manually after finishing work and check your Linked Devices regularly. Have you checked your active WhatsApp Web sessions this week? Comment SAFETY for the full safety checklist.

Fraudsters in Boss Scam send malicious ZIP files like Statement of Account.zip to hijack WhatsApp Web sessions and demand urgent transfers.
The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) alerted over 58,000 potential victims about WhatsApp account takeover fraud.

piece.dm_text:
Here is the MHA WhatsApp Web security checklist for your business:
1. Closing browser tab does NOT log you out. Manually click Log Out after every session.
2. Never open unknown attachments like Statement of Account.zip, RBI.zip or MCA.zip containing executable malware.
3. Open WhatsApp on phone -> Settings -> Linked Devices and log out of any unrecognized or old computer sessions.
4. If using WhatsApp Web on shared office computers is necessary, use Incognito or Private browsing mode.
5. Always verify urgent payment requests received on WhatsApp through a direct phone call before transferring funds.

[7] TechCrunch AI — UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security
URL: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/24/uk-warns-ai-driven-cyberattacks-are-exposing-years-of-weak-security/
Image Credits: Lino Mirgele / Getty Images Security UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security Zack Whittaker 10:02 AM PST · November 24, 2026 The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.
The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) said it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post .
The NCSC says that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.
The rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds.
While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices.
“Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote.
The unit said that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data.
The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.”
The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes.

[82] YourStory — Log out after using WhatsApp Web to prevent account hijacking: MHA advises users
URL: https://yourstory.com/2026/11/mha-warns-whatsapp-web-users-of-account-hijacking-advises-logging-out-after-every-session
Log out after using WhatsApp Web to prevent account hijacking: MHA advises users | YourStory Sidebar is Loading... ADVERTISEMENT The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has issued a cybersecurity advisory cautioning users about the potential misuse of authenticated WhatsApp Web sessions to gain access to their accounts.
The advisory, dated November 18, was issued by the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit of the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), under the MHA.
The advisory warned that leaving accounts logged in on office computers or shared devices could expose them to unauthorised access. This could allow malicious actors to read private messages, send messages while impersonating the account holder, access contacts and group conversations, and exploit trusted identities to carry out fraud, phishing and social-engineering attacks.
The advisory recommends that organisations avoid using WhatsApp Web on office computers, particularly in official and sensitive environments. Users have been advised against exchanging government, financial, confidential or other sensitive information through WhatsApp Web sessions on computers.
The I4C has cautioned that simply closing a browser window or tab should not be treated as logging out of WhatsApp Web. Users must manually terminate their sessions after completing their work and avoid leaving accounts permanently logged in.
If access is unavoidable, the agency recommends using 'incognito' or 'private browsing' mode on a trusted computer, followed by a manual logout. Users have also been advised against accessing WhatsApp Web through cyber cafes, public kiosks, hotel business centres, borrowed computers, or other untrusted systems.
The advisory further recommends keeping devices, operating systems, browsers and security software updated, avoiding suspicious downloads, and monitoring accounts for unexpected messages or unusual activity.
WhatsApp Web sessions targeted in 'Boss Scam'
The latest warning comes amid a rise in WhatsApp-linked account takeover fraud. In an August 7 advisory, the MHA warned corporates and finance professionals about a campaign known as the 'Boss Scam' or CEO impersonation fraud.
According to the ministry's statement published on the Press Information Bureau, fraudsters circulated malicious ZIP files disguised as account statements and regulatory communications, using names such as 'Statement of Account.zip', 'RBI.zip' and 'MCA.zip'.
The files contained malicious Windows executable (.exe) and Dynamic Link Library (.dll) files. Once extracted and executed on a Windows computer, the malware could compromise the device and hijack an active WhatsApp Web session.
Attackers subsequently used compromised accounts to circulate the same malicious files to contacts and groups. In more advanced cases, they impersonated senior executives and instructed finance employees to make urgent transfers to fraudulent bank accounts.
The MHA said it had alerted more than 58,000 potential victims through SMS messages sent under the header 'I4CMHA-G' in the preceding 30 days. More than 10,000 Indians had been protected through coordinated interventions, including the blocking of malicious infrastructure through the government's Sahyog Portal.
The ministry also said it had shared malware-related threat intelligence with the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), Microsoft Defender, and Indian cybersecurity companies, including Quick Heal, K7 Computing and Net Protector.
In its June 22 advisory, the I4C had first flagged the emerging 'Boss Scam' threat, warning that compromised WhatsApp accounts could be used to target employees with fraudulent financial instructions.
The MHA has advised users to regularly review the 'Linked Devices' section in WhatsApp and remove unfamiliar or inactive sessions. It has also urged companies to independently verify urgent payment instructions received through messaging platforms.
